For synthetic division to work, we need the coefficient of $x$ in the denominator to be equal to $1.$ So first, we factor the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{2x+1} & =\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{2(x+\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Carrying out the synthetic division process on $$
\displaystyle \frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})},
$$ we arrive at the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 8 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\  & ↓ & -4 & 0 & 1 \\  & 8 & 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})} & =\frac{1}{2}(8{x}^{2}-2) \\  & =4{x}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}

$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{2x+1} & =\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{2(x+\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Carrying out the synthetic division process on $$
\displaystyle \frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})},
$$ we arrive at the following:

$$
\begin{array}{c|rrrr} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 8 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\  & ↓ & -4 & 0 & 1 \\ \hline  & 8 & 0 & -2 & 0\end{array}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})} & =\frac{1}{2}(8{x}^{2}-2) \\  & =4{x}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{8{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-2x-1}{2x+1}=4{x}^{2}-1.

$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $3,$ then we will get a $-3y$ term that can cancel with the $3y$ in the second equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y &=6 && |\,\times 3 \\ 2x+3y &=2\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3x-3y &=18 \\ 2x+3y &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{f(x)}{x+2}=4{x}^{2}+1
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=(x+2)(4{x}^{2}+1).
$$

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of $4{x}^{2}+1=0$ is 

$$
D=(0)^{2}-4(4)(1)=-16<0,
$$

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=-2.$

$$
